The Zubair oilfield near Basra, March 9, 2026 [Essam al-Sudani/Reuters]By Mohammad MansourPublished On 15 Nov 202615 Nov 2026
The Iraqi government has launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the Jurf al-Sakhar area, a stronghold of Iran-linked militias near Baghdad.
The campaign has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of top security directors, the Babil police chief and the director of the Oil Pipelines Company at the Ministry of Oil.

While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds from a widespread smuggling network, analysts believe the move is a highly calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into the state apparatus.
At the heart of this confrontation is Jurf al-Sakhar – also known as Jurf al-Nasr – a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah group, believed to have close links to Iran.
For over a decade, Jurf al-Nasr has allegedly harboured illicit oil refineries. An intelligence report released last week claimed that the area was at the centre of a major corruption scheme involving oil revenues and Iran-linked militias.

Al Jazeera English celebrates the 20th anniversary of its launch [Screenshot/Al Jazeera]
Twenty years ago today, on November 15, 2006, Al Jazeera English began broadcasting with a belief that the world needed a different perspective on the news. A perspective that would bring underreported stories to international attention and give people everywhere a greater opportunity to be seen and heard.
As we celebrate our 20th anniversary, that belief remains as important as ever.
The world has changed enormously over the past two decades. We have witnessed wars, political upheavals, economic crises, technological revolutions and profound changes in how people consume information. Through it all, Al Jazeera English has sought to do more than report events. We have worked to explain why they matter, explore their impact on people’s lives and help audiences understand an increasingly complex world.
Our journey has never simply been about building another international news channel. It has been about broadening the global conversation.
A different perspective on the world
From the beginning, Al Jazeera English sought to broaden international news coverage by bringing greater diversity of perspectives, voices and stories to audiences around the world.
We believed that events everywhere deserved attention, depth and serious journalism, regardless of where they took place. We also believed that people experiencing conflict, injustice, poverty and political change should not be merely subjects of news coverage, but voices within it.

Spain has declared a migration emergency in the Canary Islands after the arrival of more than 9,000 people in its Atlantic Ocean territory since the start of November.
Spain’s Maritime Rescue Service said it had rescued 1,488 migrants aboard 14 dinghies, also known as pirogues, most of whom arrived on El Hierro in the Canary Islands from West Africa on Saturday.

That’s broken the record of 1,461 people rescued six years earlier in November 2020.
Spain’s Territorial Policy Minister Angel Victor Torres is visiting ⁠El Hierro on Sunday to discuss the surge in migrant arrivals.
Al Jazeera’s Bernard Smith, reporting from El Hierro, said the arrival this year has set a record in the 32 years since statistics have been collected.

item.title: Twenty Years of Al Jazeera English: The Counternarrative
item.description:
play video
play video
Video Duration 47 minutes 22 seconds play-arrow
47:22
Two decades of AJE: Shaping media, amplifying unheard voices and driving global conversations.Read more
In November 2006, Al Jazeera English went live with an audacious mandate: to challenge the traditional hegemony of Western media conglomerates and structurally invert the global news flow by providing a localised, uncompromising perspective from the Global South to the English-speaking world. To mark its 20th anniversary, this documentary delivers a definitive, multilayered chronicle of AJE’s trajectory from a disruptive alternative to dominant Western news media to the globally consumed news source it is today. The film seamlessly pairs an outside-in investigative lens with ground-up human testimony and internal insights. The film reflects on AJE’s historic coverage of global conflicts, the climate crisis, genocide and more in a drastically changing media landscape, all while balancing difficult decisions regarding where to focus resources, battling stigma as state-funded media and weathering the targeting of the channel’s journalists and bureaus while trying to remain true to AJE’s core principles.Published On 15 Nov 202615 Nov 2026

A historic catch - Starship returns to the launchpad in Starbase, Texas [Steve Nesius/Reuters]By Priyanka ShankarPublished On 15 Nov 202615 Nov 2026
On a cloudy Saturday afternoon in the southern US state of Texas, a pair of large metallic arms stretched out and caught a giant in midair as it descended from the sky.
At 124 metres (407ft) tall, SpaceX’s Starship is the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, intended for travel to the Moon and Mars. Yet 22 hours after its latest blast off into space, it made history on Earth while returning, as it slipped smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 at Starbase city in Texas.

Aerospace engineers across the globe have lauded the first-ever capture of the upper stage of a spaceship and welcomed the achievement, which signals that mega rockets could soon be fully reusable.
Here’s why the historic capture matters:
How did it work?
On Saturday, after orbiting Earth 14 times for 22.5 hours, SpaceX’s Starship emerged from thick clouds over its Starbase launch site, flipped itself to a vertical position and slowly descended into the arms on the ‘Mechazilla’ launch tower.
Like massive tweezers, the arms caught the upper stage of the spacecraft in midair, while its engines were still roaring.
The spacecraft then hooked onto the tower’s mechanical arms and shut off its engines.

Israel’s caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his appeal for a unity government with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, casting a coalition that would keep him in power as integral to Israel’s national security.
In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said his meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”. He said such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all” and claimed Tehran would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.

Who: Germany vs Netherlands

Where: Olympiastadion in Berlin, Germany

How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:45 GMT before our live text commentary stream.
Germany and the Netherlands head into the final Group A2 Nations League match hoping to secure their place in the quarterfinals.
Xavi Hernandez’s Netherlands side are practically through – barring a huge swing in goal difference – as they lead the table with 11 points after thrashing Greece 7-0 on Friday.
Jurgen Klopp’s Germany, who beat bottom placed Serbia 3-1 in their last game, know they will likely need a win to progress.
The Germans sit third with eight points, level with second-placed Greece but below them on their head-to-head record, which trumps goal difference as a tiebreaker in this season’s competition. Greece host Serbia, who have yet to win a point.
What happened in Germany’s last game?
Germany cruised to a 3-1 win against Serbia in Belgrade on Friday.
The Germans forced Serbia’s Srdan Babic into an early own goal with Florian Wirtz and Brajan Gruda also scoring.
Babic made up for his blunder with a second-half consolation strike while Serbia finished with nine men after substitutes Vanja Dragojevic and Andrija Zivkovic were sent off late on.
